0.title: In the Beginning, and What Went Wrong
0.overview:
The first three chapters of the Bible answer the deepest questions human beings ask. Where did everything come from? Who are we? Why is the world so beautiful and yet so broken? Why do we die? Is there any hope?

Genesis answers that a good and all-powerful God created everything from nothing. He made human beings in his own image, male and female, to know him, love him and rule his world under him. But the first man and woman rebelled, and sin and death entered the world. Every page of Scripture that follows is the story of how God sets out to undo the damage, and it begins with a promise in Genesis 3:15.

These chapters are also among the most debated in the Bible. How long were the days of creation? Was Adam a real man? How does Genesis relate to modern science? This study sets out the main views on these questions fairly and then gives a verdict. But its main aim is not to win arguments. It is to help us worship the Creator, understand ourselves and see our need of the Saviour.

Six units: (1) In the Beginning, God; (2) Six Days; (3) Made in God's Image; (4) Adam: The First Man; (5) The Fall; (6) The First Gospel.

1.title: In the Beginning, God
1.overview:
In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth (Gen 1:1). The Bible's first sentence is its foundation. Before anything existed, God was. He did not need the world; he created it freely.

Out of nothing. God did not shape pre-existing material, as an artist works with clay. He spoke, and things came to be. By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible (Heb 11:3). For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm (Ps 33:9).

By the Trinity. The Father created through the Son, the eternal Word, by the Spirit. All things were made through him (John 1:3). For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible (Col 1:16). The Spirit hovered over the waters (Gen 1:2).

Good. Again and again in Genesis 1, God saw that what he had made was good. At the end, God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good (Gen 1:31). The physical world is not evil or unimportant. Matter, bodies, food, beauty and work are God's good gifts.

Ordered. Genesis 1 shows God bringing order out of formlessness. On the first three days he forms realms: light and darkness, sky and sea, land and plants. On the next three days he fills them: sun, moon and stars; birds and fish; animals and humanity. The world is not random. It reflects the mind of a wise Creator.

For his glory. The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork (Ps 19:1). Creation exists to display God's power, wisdom and goodness. And it continues only because he sustains it: in him all things hold together (Col 1:17).
1.theology:
Creator and creature: The most basic distinction in reality is between God and everything else. Creation is not part of God, as pantheism teaches, nor is it independent of God, as deism imagines. It depends on him every moment.

Against the myths: The nations around Israel told creation stories full of warring gods, with the world made from a dead god's body and humans made as slaves. Genesis is strikingly different: one God, no struggle, a good world and human beings made with dignity in his image.

Creation and science: Because God made an ordered world and made us able to understand it, science is possible and good. Christians need not fear honest science. But Scripture, not changing theories, is our final authority about origins.
1.examples:
Then: When Paul preached in Athens to philosophers who worshipped many gods, he began with creation: The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man (Acts 17:24). The doctrine of creation was his starting point for the gospel.

Now: A teenager is told at school that the universe is an accident and human life has no meaning. Reading Genesis 1 and Psalm 19 with his father, he begins to see the world differently. The stars are not meaningless; they declare God's glory. And he is not an accident; he was made by God and for God.

A simple test: When you look at the natural world, do you see it as an accident or as the handiwork of God?

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters. And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. And God saw that the light was good. And God separated the light from the darkness. God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, the first day. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The first verse names the Creator and the creation. The earth begins formless and empty, and the Spirit hovers over the waters. Then God speaks: Let there be light. Creation happens by God's word. He separates light from darkness and names them. The first day is complete.

verseByVerse.quote: By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host. He gathers the waters of the sea as a heap; he puts the deeps in storehouses. Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him! For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalmist celebrates creation by God's word and breath. He gathered the seas and stored the deeps. All the earth should fear him, because he spoke and it came to be. Creation is a reason for awe and worship.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Faith understands what eyes cannot see: the universe was created by the word of God. The visible world came from the invisible God. This is the first example of faith in the great chapter on faith, because everything else depends on it.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him. And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul identifies the Son as the agent of creation. All things, visible and invisible, were created by him, through him and for him. He is before all things, and he holds everything together. Creation was made by Christ and for Christ.

1.reflection:
What does it mean that God created "out of nothing"?

How does the goodness of creation shape your view of the physical world?

Read Psalm 19:1-6. How does creation declare God's glory?

How does the doctrine of creation give meaning to your life?

2.title: Six Days
2.overview:
Genesis 1 describes creation in six days, followed by a seventh day of rest. How should we read these days? This question has become one of the most debated in the church, especially since the rise of modern geology and evolutionary theory.

What the text says. Each day is described with the phrase And there was evening and there was morning, followed by a number: the first day, the second day and so on. Later, the fourth commandment grounds Israel's weekly rhythm in the creation week: For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day (Exod 20:11). The plain reading is a week of ordinary days.

Mature creation. God made Adam as a grown man, not an infant, and trees bearing fruit. A creation made in six days would have been functional and mature from the start.

From the beginning. Jesus said, But from the beginning of creation, "God made them male and female." (Mark 10:6). He speaks as if humanity was present at the beginning of creation, not after billions of years of history.

Death before the fall? Scripture links death to sin: sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin (Rom 5:12). Creation was subjected to futility and is in bondage to corruption (Rom 8:20-21) because of the fall. Many Christians believe this rules out long ages of animal death, disease and suffering before Adam's sin, since God called his creation very good.

Charity. Faithful Christians who love the Bible hold different views on this question. It is not a test of salvation. We should hold our convictions firmly and humbly, and treat those who differ as brothers and sisters.
2.theology:
The views. The "day-age" view reads each day as a long age, matching the scientific timescale. The "framework" view sees the days as a literary structure arranging creation topically, not chronologically. The "analogical" view sees them as God's work-days, analogous to ours but not identical in length. "Theistic evolution" holds that God created through an evolutionary process over billions of years, often treating Adam as a representative figure rather than the first man. The "six-day" view holds that God created in six ordinary days.

The verdict: The six-day reading is the most faithful to the text. The days are numbered and marked by evening and morning. Exodus 20:11 grounds the human week on God's week. Jesus and Paul treat Adam as a real first man at the beginning of creation. And the link between sin and death fits a creation without death before the fall. The other views are held by godly Christians, but they arise largely from pressure outside the text. Scripture, not changing scientific consensus, should govern our reading.

What matters most: On every view held by orthodox Christians, God is Creator, creation is good, humanity is made in his image and sin entered through the fall. These are the non-negotiables.
2.examples:
Then: In the fourth commandment, God told Israel to work six days and rest on the seventh, because that is what he did (Exod 20:8-11). Israel's weekly calendar was a reminder of creation. Every Sabbath pointed back to the beginning.

Now: A university student studying biology feels torn between her faith and her lectures. She meets an older Christian scientist who takes the six-day view. He does not mock her questions or pretend they are easy. He helps her see that Scripture is her final authority, that science has limits when it speaks of unrepeatable past events, and that many questions remain open. She leaves with her faith strengthened and her mind still curious.

A simple test: Do you let Scripture shape how you read science, or science shape how you read Scripture?

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done. So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God had seen everything he made, and it was very good, and the sixth day ended (Gen 1:31). Then God finished his work and rested on the seventh day, blessing it and making it holy. The pattern of six days of work and one of rest begins here, in God's own work.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates. For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The fourth commandment roots Israel's week in the creation week. Six days of labour and a day of rest, because in six days the LORD made heaven and earth and rested on the seventh. The argument assumes that God's days and Israel's days correspond.

verseByVerse.quote: But from the beginning of creation, 'God made them male and female.' 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.' So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus answers a question about divorce by going back to creation. From the beginning of creation God made them male and female. Jesus treats Genesis 1 and 2 as real history, and places humanity at the beginning of creation.

verseByVerse.quote: For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Creation waits eagerly for the revealing of God's children. It was subjected to futility, not willingly, but in hope. It will be set free from its bondage to corruption. The whole creation groans. The present brokenness of nature is linked to the fall, and it will be undone.

2.reflection:
What are the main views on the days of Genesis 1? What are the strengths of each?

Why does Exodus 20:11 matter for how we read Genesis 1?

How does Romans 5:12 and 8:20-22 bear on the question of death before the fall?

How can Christians who disagree on this question show charity to one another?

3.title: Made in God's Image
3.overview:
Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth." (Gen 1:26). Human beings are unique in creation. Only they are made in God's image.

What the image means. Scripture does not give a simple definition, but it shows several aspects. We are made to know God and relate to him. We have reason, moral awareness, creativity and the capacity for love. We are made to rule creation as God's representatives, like the statues ancient kings set up to show their rule. And we are made as male and female, in relationship.

Dignity. Every human being bears God's image: rich and poor, young and old, born and unborn, healthy and disabled, of every nation and race. This is the foundation of human dignity and human rights. It is why murder is so serious: Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image (Gen 9:6). It is why even cursing someone is wrong (Jas 3:9).

Dominion. God gave humanity a task: Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion (Gen 1:28). This is not permission to exploit, but a calling to care for and develop the world as God's stewards. Adam was put in the garden to work it and keep it (Gen 2:15). Work, science, art and culture are part of this calling.

Marred, not erased. After the fall, the image of God remains (Gen 9:6; Jas 3:9), but it is defaced. We still have dignity, but our minds, hearts and wills are corrupted by sin.

Restored in Christ. Christ is the image of the invisible God (Col 1:15). Believers are being renewed in knowledge after the image of their Creator (Col 3:10) and conformed to the image of the Son (Rom 8:29).
3.theology:
Male and female: The image is borne by both men and women equally. Their differences are part of God's good design, not a barrier to equality. The Biblical Sexuality study explores this further.

Body and soul: God formed man from the dust and breathed into him the breath of life (Gen 2:7). Humans are not souls trapped in bodies, nor merely bodies. We are unified persons, body and soul.

Racism: Since all humans descend from one man (Acts 17:26) and bear God's image, racism is a denial of the doctrine of creation. There is one human race.
3.examples:
Then: David, looking at the night sky, marvelled that God would care for human beings. Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor (Ps 8:5). Human beings are small, but crowned.

Now: A nurse in a care home looks after elderly residents with dementia. Some cannot speak or recognise anyone. She treats each one with gentleness and respect, because she sees in them the image of God. Her colleagues notice the difference.

A simple test: Is there a group of people you find it hard to see as bearing God's image? What would change if you did?

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth." So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. And God blessed them. And God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God speaks within himself: Let us make man in our image. Humanity is created male and female, blessed and given dominion. Of all creation, only human beings are made in God's image and given this calling. Our identity and our purpose come from God.

verseByVerse.quote: When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him? Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor. You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, whatever passes along the paths of the seas. O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David compares the vastness of the heavens with the smallness of man. Yet God has crowned humanity with glory and honour and placed all creation under its feet. Hebrews applies this psalm to Christ, the true man who fulfils humanity's calling (Heb 2:6-9).

verseByVerse.quote: And for your lifeblood I will require a reckoning: from every beast I will require it and from man. From his fellow man I will require a reckoning for the life of man. "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. And you, be fruitful and multiply, increase greatly on the earth and multiply in it." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: After the flood, God renews the command to be fruitful and establishes the sanctity of human life. Murder is an attack on God's image. The image remains even in a fallen world, and it is the reason human life is precious.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator. Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Believers have put off the old self and put on the new, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its Creator. In this new humanity, ethnic and social divisions no longer define us. Christ is all, and in all. Salvation restores the image of God.

3.reflection:
What does it mean to you that you are made in God's image?

How does the image of God shape your view of the unborn, the disabled and the elderly?

What does "dominion" over creation mean, and what does it not mean?

How is the image of God being restored in you through Christ?

4.title: Adam: The First Man
4.overview:
Genesis 2 zooms in on the creation of the first man and woman. Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature (Gen 2:7). God shaped him personally and gave him life by his own breath.

The garden. God planted a garden in Eden and placed the man there to work it and keep it. He gave him freedom to eat of every tree, with one exception: the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die (Gen 2:17). The test was simple: would Adam trust God's word?

The woman. God saw that it was not good for the man to be alone. He made the woman from the man's side and brought her to him. Adam's joy was immediate. Marriage began with God's gift.

A real man. The rest of Scripture treats Adam as a historical person. Genesis 5 lists his descendants and his age. Luke traces Jesus' genealogy back to Adam, the son of God (Luke 3:38). Paul tells the Athenians that God made from one man every nation of mankind (Acts 17:26). Most importantly, Paul builds his teaching on sin and salvation on a comparison between Adam and Christ.

Adam and Christ. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive (1 Cor 15:22). Adam was a representative head: when he sinned, all humanity fell with him. Christ is the second Adam: through his obedience, all who are in him are made righteous. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous (Rom 5:19). If there was no first Adam, Paul's argument about the second Adam loses its foundation.
4.theology:
A historical Adam: the views. Some Christians, often influenced by evolutionary science, see Adam as a symbol of humanity, or as one representative chosen from a larger population. The historic Christian view is that Adam and Eve were real individuals, specially created by God, from whom all humanity descends.

The verdict: The historic view is right. Genesis presents Adam in genealogies alongside other historical figures. Jesus treats the creation of the first couple as history (Matt 19:4-6). Luke and Paul trace humanity to one man. And the gospel itself depends on the parallel between the real first Adam and the real second Adam.

Federal headship: Reformed theology describes Adam as the covenant head of humanity. God dealt with him as our representative, so his fall became ours. This can seem unfair, but the same principle is what allows Christ to represent us and save us. The Covenant Theology study explains this further.
4.examples:
Then: In Romans 5, Paul compares Adam and Christ point by point. Through Adam came sin, condemnation and death. Through Christ come grace, justification and life. And grace abounds even more than sin (Rom 5:20). The story of the first Adam prepares us for the better story of the second.

Now: A Christian reads that many scholars consider Adam a myth. He wonders whether it matters. Studying Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, he sees that the whole gospel is built on two men, Adam and Christ. If one is a myth, what about the other? He becomes convinced that Adam's history matters.

A simple test: Can you explain how Adam and Christ are compared in Romans 5?

verseByVerse.quote: then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature. And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed. And out of the ground the LORD God made to spring up every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food. The tree of life was in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God forms the man from dust and breathes life into him. He plants a garden full of beautiful and fruitful trees, including the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Humanity begins in intimacy with God, in a place of beauty and provision.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it. And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God puts the man in the garden to work and keep it. He gives generous freedom, with one prohibition and a solemn warning. The command tests whether Adam will trust and obey God's word. Everything that follows hangs on his response.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned— for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law. Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come. But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. And the free gift is not like the result of that one man's sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification. For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ. Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul draws the great parallel. Sin and death came through one man, Adam. Righteousness and life come through one man, Jesus Christ. Adam's one trespass led to condemnation for all; Christ's one act of righteousness leads to justification and life. The gift is far greater than the trespass.

verseByVerse.quote: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Christ has been raised as the firstfruits of those who have died. Death came through a man; resurrection comes through a man. As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. The two Adams stand at the head of two humanities.

4.reflection:
Why does it matter that Adam was a real historical person?

Read Romans 5:12-21. List the contrasts between Adam and Christ.

What does it mean that Adam was humanity's representative?

How does Christ, the second Adam, succeed where the first Adam failed?

5.title: The Fall
5.overview:
Genesis 3 is one of the saddest chapters in the Bible. It explains why the world is the way it is.

The temptation. The serpent, crafty and deceitful, began by questioning God's word: Did God actually say, "You shall not eat of any tree in the garden"? (Gen 3:1). Then he denied God's warning: You will not surely die. Then he slandered God's motives, suggesting God was holding back something good (Gen 3:4-5). The woman saw that the tree was good for food, a delight to the eyes and desirable to make one wise. She ate, and gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate (Gen 3:6).

The result. Their eyes were opened, but not as they had hoped. They knew they were naked and felt shame. They hid from God among the trees. When God called, Where are you? (Gen 3:9), Adam blamed the woman, and the woman blamed the serpent. Fellowship with God was broken, and so was trust between them.

The curse. God pronounced judgment. The serpent was cursed. The woman would bear children in pain, and conflict would mark her relationship with her husband. The ground was cursed because of Adam, so that work would become toil. And death would come: for you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19). Finally, they were driven out of the garden, away from the tree of life.

The effects on all. Adam's sin was not only his own. Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned (Rom 5:12). Every human being is born with a sinful nature, separated from God and under condemnation. Paul describes the natural state of humanity: dead in the trespasses and sins, following the world and the devil, by nature children of wrath (Eph 2:1-3).

A broken world. The fall affected all of creation. Disease, disaster, decay and death are all symptoms of a world under the curse. Relationships, societies and nature itself are bent out of shape.
5.theology:
Original sin: Original sin means two things. First, Adam's guilt is counted to all humanity, because he was our representative. Second, every person inherits a corrupt nature, inclined toward sin from birth (Ps 51:5). We are not sinners because we sin; we sin because we are sinners.

Total depravity: This does not mean people are as bad as they could be. It means sin has affected every part of us: mind, will, emotions and body. No part is untouched, and we cannot save ourselves. The Doctrines of Grace study treats this more fully.

Why did God allow it? Scripture does not fully answer this. But it shows that God was not taken by surprise. Christ was the Lamb foreknown before the foundation of the world (1 Pet 1:20). God permitted the fall in order to display his grace, justice and glory in a way that would not otherwise have been seen.
5.examples:
Then: In Genesis 4, the effects of the fall spread quickly. Cain, the first son, murdered his brother Abel out of jealousy (Gen 4:8). By Genesis 6, every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually (Gen 6:5). Sin is not static; it grows.

Now: A Christian watching the news feels overwhelmed by violence, injustice and suffering. Reading Genesis 3, he understands that this is not how the world was meant to be. The brokenness is real, and it has a cause. But Genesis 3 also contains a promise, and that gives him hope.

A simple test: Where do you see the effects of the fall in your own heart and life today?

verseByVerse.quote: Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?" And the woman said to the serpent, "We may eat of the fruit of the trees in the garden, but God said, 'You shall not eat of the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of the garden, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.'" But the serpent said to the woman, "You will not surely die. For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil." So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate. Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The serpent's strategy is subtle. He questions, denies and slanders. The woman looks, desires and takes. Adam, who was with her, eats. Their eyes are opened, but what they see is their shame. Sin promises knowledge and freedom, and delivers shame and separation.

verseByVerse.quote: And they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, "Where are you?" And he said, "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." He said, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?" The man said, "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate." Then the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this that you have done?" The woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God comes walking in the garden. The man and woman hide. God calls, Where are you?, not because he does not know, but to draw them out. Adam blames the woman and, by implication, God who gave her. The woman blames the serpent. Sin breaks our relationship with God and with each other.

verseByVerse.quote: To the woman he said, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you." And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field. By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The consequences of the fall touch the deepest parts of life: childbearing, marriage, work and death. Pain, conflict, toil and dust. Yet even in judgment, God does not destroy them immediately. He lets them live, and the story continues.

verseByVerse.quote: And you were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience— among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul describes humanity's condition after the fall. Dead in sins, following the world and the devil, living in the passions of the flesh, by nature children of wrath. This is a grim picture. But the next verse begins with two great words: But God (Eph 2:4).

5.reflection:
How did the serpent tempt the woman? How does temptation still work this way?

What were the effects of the fall on humanity's relationship with God, each other and creation?

What does "original sin" mean?

Read Ephesians 2:1-10. How does "But God" change everything?

6.title: The First Gospel
6.overview:
In the middle of the curse, God gave a promise. Speaking to the serpent, he said, I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel (Gen 3:15). This has been called the first gospel: the first announcement of the good news.

A coming deliverer. God promised that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent's head. There would be conflict, and the deliverer would be wounded, but the serpent would be defeated. The rest of the Old Testament traces this line of promise through Seth, Noah, Abraham, Judah and David.

Fulfilled in Christ. Jesus is the offspring of the woman, born of Mary. At the cross, the serpent struck his heel; Christ died. But by that death he crushed the serpent's head, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Heb 2:14). Paul echoes Genesis 3:15: The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (Rom 16:20).

Clothed by God. After the fall, Adam and Eve tried to cover themselves with fig leaves. God made them garments of skins and clothed them (Gen 3:21). An animal died so that their shame could be covered. It is a picture of what God would do in Christ, clothing sinners in his righteousness.

Paradise restored. Adam and Eve were driven from the garden and the tree of life. At the end of the Bible, the tree of life reappears, by the river of the water of life, in the new Jerusalem. No longer will there be anything accursed (Rev 22:3). What was lost in Eden is restored, and more, in the new creation.

A new creation now. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Cor 5:17). The God who said Let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6). Salvation is a new act of creation.
6.theology:
The seed line: Genesis 3:15 sets up a conflict that runs through the whole Bible: the offspring of the woman against the offspring of the serpent. It is seen in Cain and Abel, Israel and the nations, and finally in Christ and Satan.

Grace before judgment: God gave the promise before he pronounced the curses on the man and woman. Grace was spoken first.

Creation, fall, redemption, consummation: The Bible's storyline moves from creation through the fall to redemption in Christ and the consummation of all things in the new creation. The Big Story of the Bible study traces this storyline in full.
6.examples:
Then: When Eve gave birth to her first son, she said, I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD (Gen 4:1). She may have hoped he was the promised deliverer. He was not; he became a murderer. The promise would wait thousands of years for its fulfilment in Christ.

Now: A woman who has made a mess of her life feels that her story is beyond repair. A friend shows her Genesis 3:15 and 21 and 2 Corinthians 5:17. Even in the garden, God had a plan of grace. She realises that the God who promised to crush the serpent can make her new.

A simple test: How does Genesis 3:15 point to Christ? Could you explain it to someone else?

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above all beasts of the field; on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life. I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God curses the serpent and announces lasting enmity between it and the woman, and between their offspring. Then comes the promise: her offspring will bruise the serpent's head, while the serpent bruises his heel. A head wound is fatal; a heel wound is not. Victory is promised, at a cost.

verseByVerse.quote: The man called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all living. And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them. Then the LORD God said, "Behold, the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever—" therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken. He drove out the man, and at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Adam names his wife Eve, because she is the mother of all living, an act of faith in God's promise. God clothes them with garments of skins. Then he sends them out of the garden, guarding the way to the tree of life. Judgment and mercy are woven together.

verseByVerse.quote: The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul ends his letter to the Romans with a promise that echoes Genesis 3:15: God will soon crush Satan under your feet. The victory won by Christ will be shared by his people. The war that began in Eden will end in triumph.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations. No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Bible ends where it began, with a garden and the tree of life. But now it is a city filled with the redeemed. The curse is gone. God's servants see his face. Everything lost in the fall is restored and surpassed in the new creation.

6.reflection:
Why is Genesis 3:15 called the "first gospel"?

How did Christ fulfil the promise of crushing the serpent's head?

What does God clothing Adam and Eve teach about salvation?

How does Revelation 22 show that what was lost in Eden will be restored?
